newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Packer pulls plug on casino deal.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Packer pulls plug on casino deal.

text.p: Australian billionaire Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL) confirmed on Saturday that it would not proceed with a A$240 million deal to buy the management contract for the Sydney Harbour Casino.

PBL had an option to buy 85 percent of the Sydney casino's management contract from U.S. based Showboat Inc. PBL also said it would not proceed with an option to buy a 10 percent stake in the casino's owner, Sydney Harbour Casino Ltd.
Newspapers speculated earlier this week that Packer would pull out of the casino deal as a prelude to making a bid for newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
PBL said it had allowed the deal to lapse because of difficulties encountered with the Casino Control Authority (CCA), the regulator of casinos in the state of New South Wales.

A PBL statement made no mention of its intentions towards Fairfax but said: "Our decision not to proceed is reinforced by a concern that this transaction would have hampered PBL's ability to achieve other key strategic initiatives under consideration."
PBL, which already owns 15 percent of Sydney-based Fairfax, owns a large stable of magazines as well as Australia's top-rating Nine Network television group.

Under current Australian law, a single proprietor is not allowed to control newspapers and television stations in the same market. However, the laws are expected to be relaxed when the government announces results of an review in the next few weeks.
PBL, about 45 percent owned by the Packer family, said it had encountered several problems with the Casino Control Authority.
PBL Chairman Brian Powers said these included the CCA's refusal to permit Showboat to provide PBL with copies of documents necessary to complete its due diligence.
Powers said that under Showboat's agreement with the CCA, the U.S. company was not permitted to disclose certain information to third parties with the CCA's consent.

"This restriction covers substantial documentation absolutely necessary for us to evaluate what we would be purchasing for A$240 million including, importantly, an amendment to Showboat's management agreement," Powers said.
"This has prevented finalisation of definitive documentation and effectively killed the proposed deal," he said.
Powers said the CCA had also informed PBL that it would not finalise the confidentiality agreement it required to release the documents unless PBL paid A$500,000.
"There is absolutely no statuatory authority for the CCA demanding a payment prior to processing the confidentiality agreement," Powers said. "We refused to pay this amount."
Powers said the CCA also had advised that it would not be able to complete all probity checks and transaction reviews for the deal within a reasonable time.
In addition, he said PBL's due diligence had shown that the CCA interfered in every aspect of the casino's operation, even in areas that had nothing to do with the CCA's statuatory charter.
"...PBL, as a company, is not well suited to manage under a regulatory regime that needlessly impedes a business' performance," Powers said.
Fairfax shares rose last week on talk of a bid by PBL but the stock eased two cents on profit-taking on Friday. At its last traded price of A$3.23, the company is valued at A$2.5 billion.
Fairfax titles include The Sydney Morning Herald, The Australian Financial Review and Melbourne's The Age newspaper.
PBL shares closed five cents down at A$6.70 on Friday, valuing the company at A$3.4 billion.
